items.q:
Statement 1: A business that sources from a single supplier faces greater supply chain risk than one that uses multiple suppliers.
Statement 2: Using a single supplier always results in higher unit costs than using multiple suppliers.
opts: Statement 1 is true. Statement 2 is true.
Statement 1 is true. Statement 2 is false.
Statement 1 is false. Statement 2 is true.
Statement 1 is false. Statement 2 is false.
items.why: Statement 1 is correct: a single supplier creates concentration risk — any disruption halts supply with no alternative. Statement 2 is false: a single supplier relationship often allows a business to negotiate lower unit costs through volume discounts and long-term contracts, so costs can be lower, not higher.
items.label: New question

items.q:
Statement 1: Operating at 100% capacity utilisation is always preferable to operating at 85% capacity utilisation.

Statement 2: Capacity utilisation is calculated as actual output divided by maximum possible output, multiplied by 100.
opts: Statement 1 is true. Statement 2 is true.
Statement 1 is true. Statement 2 is false.
Statement 1 is false. Statement 2 is true.
Statement 1 is false. Statement 2 is false.
items.why: Statement 1 is false: 100% utilisation leaves no slack for maintenance, unexpected demand or quality checks, and can increase unit costs through overtime and breakdowns. Statement 2 correctly states the standard formula for capacity utilisation.
items.label: New question

items.q: Handy's culture emphasising problem-solving using employees from different parts of the organisation:
opts: Person culture
Power culture
Role culture
Task culture
items.why: Task culture is project/team-based, bringing together people from different departments to solve specific problems. It's flexible and team-oriented. Task culture = cross-functional project teams. Different from role culture (rigid departments) or power culture (one boss).
items.label: Past paper question

items.q: A factory produces 4,800 units per week using 60 workers. After a reorganisation, the same 60 workers produce 5,400 units per week. What is the labour productivity after the reorganisation?
opts: 80 units per worker per week
90 units per worker per week
96 units per worker per week
108 units per worker per week
items.why: Labour productivity = output ÷ number of workers = 5,400 ÷ 60 = 90 units per worker per week. A common error is to divide by the original output or to use the increase in output rather than the total.
items.label: New question

items.q: Payables are the value of:
opts: A firm's overdraft
Inventory held by a business
Money owed to a firm by customers
Money owed to suppliers by a business
items.why: Payables (trade payables/creditors) = money the business owes TO its suppliers for goods/services purchased on credit. Payables = what you owe to suppliers. Receivables = what customers owe to you.
items.label: Past paper question

items.q: Which of the following conditions is most essential for a just-in-time production system to operate effectively?
opts: A large buffer stock held in reserve at all times to ensure production can continue uninterrupted if supplier deliveries are delayed or demand unexpectedly increases.
Reliable suppliers who can deliver small quantities at short notice.
A workforce paid on a piece-rate basis to incentivise faster output and ensure production targets are consistently met without the need for excess inventory.
High capacity utilisation of at least 95% to ensure that machinery and labour are fully occupied and that the cost per unit remains as low as possible throughout the year.
items.why: JIT depends entirely on receiving the right materials at the right time — without reliable, responsive suppliers the system collapses because there is no buffer stock to absorb late deliveries. Buffer stock, piece-rate pay and near-maximum utilisation are not requirements of JIT.
items.label: New question

items.q: A company relies only on decision trees. If decisions are based on the financial outcome, what is the most important factor?
opts: Expected value
Initial cost
Net gain
Probability of success
items.why: Net gain is the most important because it represents the financial benefit after deducting the initial cost. Net gain = Expected Value - Initial Cost. Expected value alone doesn't account for how much you invested. Two projects with the same EV but different costs look identical - which is misleading.
items.label: Past paper question

items.q: Which of the following is the best example of 'overproduction' as a form of waste identified in lean production?
opts: Workers waiting for components to arrive before they can continue assembly.
Manufacturing 2,000 units when customer orders only exist for 1,400 units.
Moving finished goods across the factory floor to reach the loading bay.
Using more raw material than the product specification requires.
items.why: Overproduction means making more than is currently demanded, tying up materials, storage space and labour. Waiting, unnecessary movement and excess material usage are separate categories of lean waste — common errors involve confusing overproduction with over-processing or excess motion.
items.label: New question

items.q: Abacus plc data: employees doubled (20 to 40), output doubled (50 to 100), capacity doubled (100 to 200). Statement 1: 'Labour productivity stayed the same.' Statement 2: 'Capacity utilisation stayed the same.'
opts: Statement 1 is true. Statement 2 is true.
Statement 1 is true. Statement 2 is false.
Statement 1 is false. Statement 2 is true.
Statement 1 is false. Statement 2 is false.
items.why: Both true. LP = output/employees: 2018 = 50/20 = 2.5, 2019 = 100/40 = 2.5. Same. CU = output/capacity: 2018 = 50/100 = 50%, 2019 = 100/200 = 50%. Same. Everything doubled proportionally. When all figures change in the same proportion, the ratios remain constant. Always calculate to verify.
items.label: Past paper question

items.q: More current liabilities than current assets. Shareholders provide 90% of capital employed. The business has:
opts: High current ratio and high gearing
High current ratio and low gearing
Low current ratio and high gearing
Low current ratio and low gearing
items.why: Current liabilities > current assets = low current ratio (below 1). Shareholders provide 90% of capital = only 10% is from non-current liabilities (debt), so gearing is low. 90% equity funding = low gearing (not highly reliant on debt). More liabilities than assets = low liquidity.
items.label: Past paper question

items.q: Vantage Engineering introduces a kaizen programme on its assembly line. Which of the following outcomes is most consistent with the principles of kaizen?
opts: Senior managers analyse production data, redesign the assembly process from the top down, and issue revised standardised procedures to workers for immediate implementation.
Workers in small teams identify and implement small, continuous improvements to their own processes.
The firm invests in new robotic machinery to replace manual assembly tasks, achieving large-scale step-change improvements in throughput and consistency.
Quality inspectors carry out weekly audits, record defect rates against agreed benchmarks, and submit detailed improvement reports to the production director for action.
items.why: Kaizen (continuous improvement) relies on the involvement of all employees, particularly front-line workers, in identifying and making incremental improvements. It is bottom-up, not top-down. Investing in new machinery and management-led redesign are not features of kaizen.
items.label: New question

items.q: A business starts using Kaizen. This should lead to:
opts: External, disruptive change
External, incremental change
Internal, disruptive change
Internal, incremental change
items.why: Kaizen = continuous improvement = small, ongoing, incremental changes initiated from within the business (internal). It's not disruptive (revolutionary) and not driven by external forces. Kaizen = Japanese for 'continuous improvement'. Small steps, not big leaps.
items.label: Past paper question

items.q: Hartley Plastics has set an operational objective of reducing unit costs by 12% over two years while maintaining its current defect rate of 0.5%. Which of the following best explains why these two objectives might conflict?
opts: Lower unit costs always require cutting the workforce, which reduces quality control, since fewer employees means fewer checks at each stage of the production process.
Achieving lower unit costs may require faster production runs that increase the defect rate.
Quality objectives are set by the marketing department, not operations, so the two targets are managed independently and cannot directly conflict with one another.
A 0.5% defect rate is already too high to be a meaningful operational objective, since world-class manufacturers typically target defect rates below 0.1% using Six Sigma methods.
items.why: Speeding up production or reducing inspection time to cut costs can lead to more defects, creating a direct trade-off between the cost and quality objectives. Option A is too absolute — cost reduction can be achieved in many ways that do not involve cutting staff.
items.label: New question

items.q: If Activity B is delayed by 6 days, the critical path:
opts: Does not change
Increases by 1 day
Increases by 5 days
Increases by 6 days
items.why: If Activity B has 1 day of float, a 6-day delay exceeds the float by 5 days. The critical path increases by the delay minus the available float = 6 - 1 = 5 days. When a non-critical activity is delayed beyond its float, the excess delay extends the project. Delay - Float = Project extension.
items.label: Past paper question

items.q:
Statement 1: A business producing large volumes of a standardised product is more likely to benefit from capital-intensive production than one producing small batches of customised goods.

Statement 2: Labour-intensive production always leads to higher unit costs than capital-intensive production.
opts: Statement 1 is true. Statement 2 is true.
Statement 1 is true. Statement 2 is false.
Statement 1 is false. Statement 2 is true.
Statement 1 is false. Statement 2 is false.
items.why: Statement 1 is true: high-volume standardised production allows the fixed cost of capital equipment to be spread across many units, making automation cost-effective. Statement 2 is false: labour-intensive production can achieve lower unit costs when volumes are low or when skilled labour adds value that machinery cannot replicate cost-effectively.
items.label: New question

items.q: Parkside Retail is expanding from 10 stores in one region to 60 stores across the UK. The board is considering decentralising buying decisions to regional managers. Which of the following is the strongest argument in favour of decentralisation in this context?
opts: Decentralisation ensures the company maintains a consistent brand image across all 60 stores by allowing regional managers to tailor merchandising and marketing to reflect the company's core identity in each area.
Regional managers are better placed to respond to local customer preferences and supplier availability.

Decentralisation reduces the need for regional managers to have strong commercial skills, since purchasing decisions are broken down into smaller, more manageable choices that require less strategic oversight.
Head office retains full control over pricing, ensuring national consistency and protecting the company's overall margin as it scales across a much larger and more diverse store portfolio.
items.why: As the business spans the whole UK, local conditions (customer tastes, local suppliers, regional competition) will vary significantly. Decentralising buying decisions allows those closest to local markets to act on this knowledge quickly. Option A describes an argument for centralisation. Option C is incorrect — decentralisation requires more capable regional managers, not fewer skills. Option D describes centralisation, not decentralisation.
items.label: New question

items.q: Receivables are the value of:
opts: A business's sales revenue
Inventory held by a business
Money owed to a business by its customers
Money owed to suppliers by a business
items.why: Receivables (trade receivables/debtors) = money owed TO the business BY its customers for goods/services sold on credit. Receivables = money coming IN (owed by customers). Payables = money going out (owed to suppliers).
items.label: Past paper question

items.q:
Statement 1: A capital-intensive production method will always produce a lower unit cost than a labour-intensive method.

Statement 2: Job production is more likely to be labour intensive than flow production.
opts: Statement 1 is true. Statement 2 is true.
Statement 1 is true. Statement 2 is false.
Statement 1 is false. Statement 2 is true.
Statement 1 is false. Statement 2 is false.
items.why: Statement 1 is false: capital-intensive production involves high fixed costs, so unit costs are only lower when output is sufficiently large to spread those costs — at low volumes it can be more expensive. Statement 2 is true: job production typically involves skilled craft workers tailoring output to individual orders, making it labour intensive, whereas flow production relies heavily on machinery and automation.
items.label: New question

items.q: Statement 1: 'Emergent strategy is unplanned, arising in response to change.' Statement 2: 'Strategic drift occurs when a planned strategy is continually modified.'
opts: Statement 1 is true. Statement 2 is true.
Statement 1 is true. Statement 2 is false.
Statement 1 is false. Statement 2 is true.
Statement 1 is false. Statement 2 is false.
items.why: Statement 1 true: emergent strategy is indeed an unplanned response to changing circumstances. Statement 2 false: strategic drift occurs when a strategy is not modified despite changing circumstances. Continually modifying strategy is the opposite of drift. Drift = not modifying strategy. Modifying strategy in response to change = good management, not drift.
items.label: Past paper question

items.q: Statement 1: 'An emergent strategy only occurs in response to external change.' Statement 2: 'Strategic drift occurs whenever a business changes a planned strategy.'
opts: Statement 1 is true. Statement 2 is true.
Statement 1 is true. Statement 2 is false.
Statement 1 is false. Statement 2 is true.
Statement 1 is false. Statement 2 is false.
items.why: Both false. Statement 1: emergent strategies can arise from internal or external changes (not only external). Statement 2: strategic drift is when a business fails to change its strategy despite changing circumstances - it's – the opposite of changing strategy. Strategic drift = not changing when you should. Changing strategy is the cure for drift, not the cause.
items.label: Past paper question
